patch.value: Changelog rows are ordered by a mutable timestamp, so a bulk maintenance pass reorders sections it never moved anything out of

Release attribution is now stamped, so a metadata write on a published item can no longer move it between changelog sections — measured directly: 3,744 relationship edges written across 1,713 closed items produced 0 release-section moves, 0 category moves, 0 items added or removed, and an identical 296,429-byte output. What it did produce was 2,454 lines of diff, entirely from rows being reordered inside the sections they never left.

The row order within a release section is still derived from a mutable timestamp, so it permutes whenever items are touched in a different sequence than they were last touched. The practical consequence falls on CI rather than on readers: changelog:pm:check compares generated output against the committed file, so any bulk maintenance pass reddens the gate even when attribution is provably stable and no item changed section. That converts a correctness gate into a chore gate, and the standard workaround — regenerate and commit — trains everyone to treat changelog diffs as noise, which is precisely the habit that lets a genuine attribution regression through unnoticed.

The fix is the same shape as the parent's, applied one level down: order rows within a section by a key that does not change when an item is edited. Candidates that already exist in the data are the close instant derived from history, the item identifier, and the title. Whichever is chosen, the property to assert is the same one the parent asserts for sections: editing metadata on an already-published item produces no changelog diff at all, not merely no section change.

Row order within a release section derives from a key that does not change when an item is edited; The drift check proves that a metadata write on an already-published item produces a byte-identical changelog, not merely an unchanged section assignment; The chosen key is deterministic across machines and across regeneration order, so two agents regenerating from the same tracker state produce identical bytes; Existing published sections are regenerated once under the new key and the resulting diff is reviewed as a one-time reordering rather than being suppressed; The ordering rule is documented where the changelog conventions live, so it is not rediscovered by the next bulk pass
Make a published changelog section byte-stable under any edit that does not change what shipped
The changelog drift gate becomes a real correctness signal instead of a chore that trains reviewers to ignore it
Removes the last source of changelog churn from governance work, completing what the attribution stamp started
Within-section row order derives from a stable key, and editing a published item produces no changelog diff at all
Attribution is now stamped, so ordering is the only remaining reason a maintenance pass touches the generated file

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Isolated 2026-08-10: this item, not release re-bucketing, is the whole of the residual changelog risk in a closed-item mutation, and it is much smaller than the convention built on top of it assumes.
Direct measurement. Starting from a tree where changelog:pm:check reported changed:false, one typed dependency row was added to one long-closed legacy item (pm-02c4, release v2026.5.1, closed_at null, updated_at 2026-07-27). The check then failed. Regenerating to a scratch path and diffing against the committed file gave the whole delta: three lines, one row, moving from line 2571 to line 2568. item_count stayed 2017 and bytes stayed 355556, byte-for-byte identical on both sides.
So section membership did not move. The row stayed inside v2026.5.1's own section and changed only its position within it, because rows sort on a mutable timestamp — exactly the defect this item names. Release-tag attribution under --all-release-tags held membership stable even though the item carries no closed_at, which is the property pm-wrbe recorded as landing 2026-07-26 and which this measurement independently confirms.
Consequence for the ordering of the whole backlog. The standing convention is that closed items must not be touched because a metadata write re-buckets long-shipped work into the current release. That was true before release-tag attribution and is no longer true. What remains is intra-section reordering, which is cosmetic and is fully healed by regenerating the changelog in the same commit — which is already the mandated flow, since regeneration is the last step of every tracker change. The terminal-record enrichment programme is therefore not blocked on pm-wrbe's closed_at backfill for changelog safety; it is blocked only on remembering to regenerate.
That was verified in practice on the same day: the strategic-ladder, parentless-lineage and apex-bypass waves wrote 220 evidence-cited typed edges across 213 items, the large majority of them terminal, and the only changelog consequence was row order inside already-shipped sections.
Two things follow for this item. First, the fix is worth more than its size suggests, because a stable intra-section sort key makes every closed-item mutation changelog-invisible and removes the last reason for the convention. The sort key must be immutable: closed_at where present, else the release-derived close instant, else id, never updated_at. Second, the reason this took nineteen days to establish is that the drift check reports only that the file is out of date and never what moved, so an order-only diff and a real attribution defect are indistinguishable without a manual diff. That diagnostic gap is now filed as pm-2f80fn.
